name: Smile training / smile mirror practice

lead: Smile training means practising your smile, usually in front of a mirror or camera, to find an expression that looks more natural and flattering in person and in photos. It is free and needs no equipment.

People practise controlling the facial muscles, for example engaging the muscles around the eyes as in a Duchenne smile. Related research covers smile types and the facial feedback hypothesis, the idea that expressions influence emotion; a 2016 multi-lab replication did not reproduce a classic 1988 finding, while a later meta-analysis reported a small effect overall. No trials of the practice itself for attractiveness were found.

paras: There is no formal protocol. People rehearse short sessions in a mirror, review photos or video of themselves, and keep the expressions that look best, often combining it with dental or grooming changes.
No documented harms were found for the practice itself.

chain: More attractive smile in person and photos
angle.text: People practise smiling in a mirror or on camera to find a more natural, flattering expression for daily life and photos. Rehearsal builds control of the facial muscles, so the expression comes more easily. It is free to try, and no trials of the practice itself were located.

lead: Smile training, or smile mirror practice, means rehearsing a smile on purpose, usually in front of a mirror or camera, so that it looks more natural, symmetrical or attractive in photos and in person. People do it to find the expression and lip and cheek positions they like best, and to make deliberate smiles feel less stiff.

Anatomical descriptions distinguish a Duchenne smile, which engages the muscle around the eye (orbicularis oculi) as well as the zygomaticus major that lifts the mouth corners, from a voluntary smile that uses only the zygomaticus major [1]. Voluntary and spontaneous smiles are reported to run through different cortical pathways, and Duchenne smiles are generally judged more sincere [2]. Practitioners of smile training often aim to bring eye engagement into a deliberate smile.

Formal smile training does exist in clinical practice. Physical-therapy smile exercises have been studied in patients recovering from jaw surgery, and structured smile training is part of rehabilitation after facial reanimation surgery [3][4][5]. Beyond these settings, no published trial of mirror practice for appearance in the general population was located. Related science covers the facial feedback hypothesis, the idea that facial expressions influence emotional experience [6][6].

paras: Anatomical descriptions distinguish a Duchenne smile, which engages the muscle around the eye as well as the mouth-corner muscles, from a voluntary smile using only the zygomaticus major [1]. Voluntary and spontaneous smiles are reported to run through different cortical pathways, and Duchenne smiles are generally judged more sincere [2]. Practitioners of smile training commonly aim to reproduce eye engagement in deliberate smiles.

The Duchenne smile is named after the French neurologist Guillaume Duchenne, who in the mid-19th century identified two smile types: one in which the zygomatic major raises the mouth corners and the orbicularis oculi raises the cheeks and forms crow's feet, and one that uses only the zygomatic major [1]. Messenger and colleagues in 2001 reported that research links Duchenne smiling to positive emotion [1]. The so-called Pan Am or Botox smile is a fake smile using only the zygomatic major, and chronic cosmetic botulinum toxin use around the eyes can prevent a Duchenne smile by paralysing the small muscles there [1].

A 1988 study by Strack, Martin and Stepper had participants hold a pen in their teeth, inducing a smile-like shape, and found they rated cartoons as funnier [6]. A 2016 registered replication across 17 labs did not find systematic effects, though a later analysis pointed to the presence of a camera as a possible methodological factor [6]. A 2019 meta-analysis of 138 studies reported small but robust effects (d about 0.2) [6]. The article describes only the weak form of the hypothesis as having substantial support [6]. Another encyclopedia summary describes results on forced smiling and mood as small or inconsistent [2].

Smiling is reported to raise perceived likability, approachability and in some summaries competence and trustworthiness, with cultural variation [1][2]. Gladstone (2002) is cited for the idea that smiling makes people seem more likable and approachable [1]. Krys and colleagues in 2016 found that in some cultures a smiling person may be judged less intelligent than the same person not smiling, which the authors linked to cultural uncertainty avoidance [1].

Smiling is more common in posed photographs in the US and France than in China or Japan, and in some cultures smiling at strangers can seem suspicious or unwelcoming [1]. Such differences mean the look people aim for in practice varies by setting.

A study of 44 adults (13 men, 31 women, mean age 22.6) who had Le Fort I and bilateral sagittal split jaw surgery tested a structured smile programme: after watching a smile-education video, patients practised for five minutes a day, starting one month after surgery and continuing for three months [3]. Comparing posed-smile photographs at one and four months after surgery, the share with average or high smile height rose from 32% to 50%, upward upper-lip curvature from 52% to 73%, and the first premolar as the most visible posterior tooth from 48% to 59%; the buccal corridor ratio fell from 14% to 11%, while smile arc did not show a significant difference [3].

In facial reanimation, where a functioning muscle is transplanted to restore a smile in people with facial paralysis, postoperative smile training was required to achieve a spontaneous smile [4]. In a series of 36 patients treated between 2000 and 2011 with spinal accessory nerve-innervated free muscle, mean smile excursion score improved from 0.5 to 3.4 and 83 percent could perform independent or spontaneous smiles after one year [4]. In 12 patients with Möbius syndrome, six with bilateral paralysis, mean smile excursion score improved from 0.7 to 3.4 out of 5 after bilateral gracilis transfers [5].

Studies of structured smile exercises exist in surgical rehabilitation: a 44-patient study after orthognathic surgery reported improvements in smile height, lip curvature and buccal corridor ratio after three months of five-minute daily practice [3], and facial reanimation series describe smile training as part of recovery [4][5]. No study has tested smile mirror practice in people without facial surgery or paralysis for attractiveness. Facial feedback research, described above, does not test smile training for appearance.

timeline.event: Strack, Martin and Stepper publish the pen-in-mouth facial feedback study [6].
A 17-lab registered replication report does not find systematic facial feedback effects [6].
A meta-analysis of 138 studies reports a small overall effect [6].
